Selon Guillaume Dostaler d’Entraide Loge: According to Guillaume Dostaler of Entraide Logement Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, several buildings in the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve neighbourhood have fallen victim to “spec-viction.”
Comme depuis plus d’une dizaine d’années: As he has for more than a decade, Pier-Paul Lefebvre stands with his arms crossed and a half-smile, behind the counter of the bar he runs in the Hochelaga-Maisonneuve neighbourhood. The half-dozen regulars around him trade anecdotes and jokes while sipping a beer or a small glass of hard liquor. “This is a little neighbourhood bar. [The customers] are neighbours, friends. I’ve been in this business for 40 years!” says the man, who was born a few streets from the establishment he manages. For the past few months, though, being behind the bar has left him with a bitter taste. He was hit with a bombshell: he learned that he would soon have to leave his business and abandon the project into which he has poured time and money.
« Je suis arrivé pour faire des rénovati: “I showed up to do renovations while we were still closed [because of the pandemic], and there was an eviction notice on my door,” he says, still in shock. In less than a week, the previous owner sold the building, and the buyer informed him that he would have to leave his space.
« Je n’ai pas dormi pendant une semaine: “I didn’t sleep for a week,” he recalls. Determined to explore every avenue open to him to save his business, he consulted a lawyer who specializes in the field. “There’s nothing to be done,” he says flatly. And Pier-Paul Lefebvre has a hard time making sense of the reason why. “A commercial lease has to be registered – published, as they say. You go see a notary or a lawyer, and it costs $1,000,” says the 61-year-old. “Why do you have to do that, when we signed [the lease] in front of a witness? Is it a disguised tax?” he wonders.
À court de solutions, il a contacté le n: Out of options, he contacted the new owner to try to negotiate an agreement. “I met with him, and I told him it was really sad news for me and that, clearly, he wasn’t in business to make friends! He answered that ‘business is business,’” the business owner recounts. “For me, [this bar] is like my pension fund. I’ve just lost the value of my business...” But what is this lease registration process? Why can’t a signature guarantee the contract?
« Le régime des baux commerciaux et celu: “The rules for commercial leases and those for residential leases are completely different,” says Annie Paillé without hesitation, a notary with 20 years of experience who specializes in commercial law. While residential leases are covered by the Civil Code of Québec and the Régie du logement can settle disputes between tenants and landlords, commercial leases are subject to a “mutual agreement” regime. This means that agreements between landlords and tenants are reached through a simple accord between the two parties, without the process being governed by legal provisions.
C’est ici que l’enregistrement du bail,: This is where lease registration, also called “publication” or “inscription,” comes into play.
« Lorsqu’un immeuble commercial est vend: “When a commercial building is sold and the leases are published in the Land Register [of Québec], it means the new buyer can’t claim that they weren’t aware of the leases,” continues Paillé, who drafts and registers commercial leases. This procedure, carried out by a notary, therefore guarantees a business tenant that they will not be evicted and that the terms of their lease will not change overnight following the sale of the building. This is where Pier-Paul Lefebvre’s failure to publish his lease hurts: because the agreement was not registered in the Land Register of Québec at the time the building was sold, the new owner had the right to terminate the contract, and the business owner could do nothing about it.
« Le propriétaire a souvent le gros bout: “The landlord often has the upper hand over a small business owner. There’s an imbalance of power, and the landlord will impose their lease and their clauses, with no room for negotiation,” explains Annie Paillé.
Guillaume Dostaler, coordonnateur à Entr: Guillaume Dostaler, coordinator at Entraide Logement Hochelaga-Maisonneuve for 25 years, echoes the notary’s view. In his experience, it is clear that commercial leaseholders are at much greater risk than residential tenants. “In situations where supply and demand have a major impact, it can hurt some business owners,” he explains. He points to the real estate overheating that has gripped Montréal for several years to explain new owners’ lack of interest in finding an agreement that could satisfy both parties, as in the case of Mr. Lefebvre’s bar. “Those who are buying right now are paying too much compared to the income [the property] brings in, and those who buy have pretty few scruples.
Dès qu’ils deviennent propriétaires, ils: As soon as they become owners, they go on a mission to throw people out and double the rents,” he laments. The expert notes that because of the real estate “frenzy,” gentrification in neighbourhoods like Hochelaga-Maisonneuve is intensifying, leading to the eviction of many business owners from their premises.
« Ça fait environ trois ans qu’on observ: “We’ve been seeing this in the neighbourhood for about three years. Practices like ‘spec-viction’ have appeared, and there are more and more of them,” he says.

Lefebvre: Months go by and, even though Mr. Lefebvre says he has “swallowed the bitter pill” when speaking about the fate of his business, his indignation is palpable in what he says. “It’s really taking advantage of ‘the little guy.’ [...] There’s no more respect for businesses that have been there for years. I paid taxes, didn’t I, with my rent! I worked here for twelve years, but we’re nothing, we get thrown out just like that,” he says with dismay.

We put in hours here and there, and in the end, we have leases that don’t really protect us.”
Pour Me Annie Paillé, rien n’indique que: According to Annie Paillé, nothing suggests this situation will change in the near future, since she sees no legislative will to better regulate commercial leases. “I’d be surprised if the Civil Code ever had a regime as developed as the one we have for residential leases,” says the notary.
